what_it_does: Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) are a cryptographic technique that lets one party prove to another that a statement is true (for instance, 'I know the password') without revealing any information about why it is true — a capability increasingly important for privacy-preserving blockchains and verifiable computation. Generating these proofs is computationally very expensive, requiring several distinct phases of heavy arithmetic (including a step called Multi-Scalar Multiplication, or MSM — essentially thousands of large-number multiplications bundled together — and Number Theoretic Transform, a kind of mathematical rearrangement operation). Existing ZKP accelerator chips are designed around individual operations, not the whole proof pipeline, so resources sit idle during phases the chip was not optimized for. LegoZK builds the chip from a set of re-configurable modular arithmetic units (specialized circuits for doing the big-number math that cryptography requires) connected by a reconfigurable on-chip routing network, so the chip's internal wiring and computation style can be reorganized between proof phases. For the slowest phase (MSM), LegoZK also introduces a new pipelined algorithm using lookup tables to dramatically speed up the bottleneck step.
